column2: Your security team needs to verify how organization policies are being applied across the resource hierarchy for a specific project. They want to see the combined effect of all inherited and locally-set policies for the constraints/gcp.resourceLocations constraint. Which gcloud command should they use?
column3: gcloud resource-manager org-policies list --project=PROJECT_ID
column4: gcloud org-policies describe constraints/gcp.resourceLocations --project=PROJECT_ID
column5: gcloud org-policies describe constraints/gcp.resourceLocations --effective --project=PROJECT_ID
column6: gcloud policy-intelligence analyze --org-policy=constraints/gcp.resourceLocations --project=PROJECT_ID
column8: The --effective flag returns the organization policy as it is evaluated at that point in the resource hierarchy with inheritance included. This shows the result of merging policies in the resource hierarchy and evaluating conditions. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/using-constraints

column2: Your organization is implementing centralized log collection for security analysis. You need to route audit logs from all projects to BigQuery for threat intelligence correlation. When routing logs to BigQuery, you observe that some log field names are modified in the destination table. You need to understand this behavior to correctly build queries that JOIN logs with IOC tables. What causes this behavior?
column3: Cloud Logging applies rules to shorten BigQuery schema field names for audit logs and certain structured payload fields when routing logs.
column4: The first log entry received by BigQuery determines the schema, causing subsequent entries with different field names to be dropped.
column5: BigQuery automatically truncates field names exceeding 128 characters to comply with column naming limitations.
column6: Log sinks automatically normalize nested JSON fields by flattening the hierarchy and renaming fields with path-based prefixes.
column8: When routing audit logs to BigQuery, Cloud Logging applies rules to shorten BigQuery schema field names for audit logs and certain structured payload fields. Understanding this transformation is essential for building accurate queries that correlate logs with IOC data. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit/best-practices

column2: Your security team needs to detect connections to a list of suspicious IP addresses that your threat intelligence team has identified. These IP addresses are not included in the built-in Event Threat Detection threat intelligence. You want to implement this detection in Security Command Center with minimal development effort. What should you do?
column3: Configure Cloud IDS with custom threat signatures for each IP address in your list to generate findings.
column4: Create an Event Threat Detection custom module using the Configurable Bad IP template with your list of suspicious IP addresses.
column5: Export VPC Flow Logs to BigQuery and create a scheduled SQL query to check for connections to your IP address list.
column6: Submit a parser improvement request to Google Cloud Customer Care to add your IP addresses to the built-in Malware: Bad IP detector.
column8: Event Threat Detection provides custom module templates that allow you to create custom detectors with your own parameters. The Configurable Bad IP custom module allows you to specify a list of suspicious IP addresses that you maintain, and findings are generated when logs indicate connections to any of your supplied IP addresses. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: Your security team has deployed Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR and needs to configure a playbook that only triggers for alerts that match specific custom conditions based on alert metadata fields not covered by standard trigger types. The playbook should trigger only when the alert name contains 'ransomware' and the severity is 'high'. Which trigger type should you configure?
column3: Product Name trigger configured with multiple product filters combined with a Flow condition.
column4: Alert Type trigger with Rule Generator field matching ransomware high severity.
column5: Tag Name trigger with pre-configured ransomware and high-severity tags.
column6: Custom Trigger with placeholder-based conditions to match specific alert metadata criteria.
column8: Custom Trigger lets you define custom placeholders for highly specific matches, such as conditions like 'if alert name INCLUDES ransomware' combined with severity conditions. This provides the flexibility needed for complex, multi-field matching scenarios. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/using-triggers-in-playbooks

column2: You are configuring Cloud DLP discovery to automatically tag BigQuery tables based on their calculated sensitivity levels. The tags will be used for IAM conditional access policies to restrict access to highly sensitive data. What should you configure in the discovery scan configuration?
column3: Enable column-level security in BigQuery and use the discovery service to automatically apply policy tags to columns containing sensitive infoTypes.
column4: Enable the Tag resources action and specify tag values for each sensitivity level including high, moderate, low, and unknown.
column5: Configure the discovery service to publish data profiles to BigQuery and create a Cloud Function that applies tags based on sensitivity scores.
column6: Create an inspection template with sensitivity thresholds and configure the discovery service to use VPC Service Controls for access restriction.
column8: The Tag resources action instructs Sensitive Data Protection to automatically attach tags to resources based on the calculated sensitivity levels. You configure tag values for each sensitivity level, and IAM conditions can then grant or deny access based on tag presence. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/dlp/docs/control-access-based-on-data-sensitivity

column2: Your security team needs to write a custom YARA-L detection rule in Google SecOps that matches file hashes against the Applied Threat Intelligence Fusion Feed. The rule should only alert when matched indicators have been associated with known threat actors. Which context entity filtering approach should you use?
column3: Filter the context graph using metadata.product_name = 'MANDIANT_FUSION_IOC' and evaluate if is_attributed returns a value of 1 or greater.
column4: Filter the context graph using metadata.vendor_name = 'GOOGLE_THREAT_INTEL' and check the active_ir boolean field.
column5: Filter the context graph using metadata.source_type = 'THREAT_INTEL' and match on confidence_score greater than 80.
column6: Filter the context graph using entity_type = 'INDICATOR' and evaluate the threat.verdict_info.severity field for 'HIGH'.
column8: The ATI Fusion Feed context entities use the product and vendor name 'MANDIANT_FUSION_IOC'. The is_attributed field returns 1 or greater when the indicator has at least one threat association of type MALWARE or THREAT_ACTOR, allowing you to filter for only attributed indicators. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-fusion-feed

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Enterprise with the SCC Enterprise – Urgent Posture Findings Connector enabled. You notice that multiple Security Health Analytics findings for the same resource type and project are creating separate cases, increasing analyst workload. You want to configure the system so related findings are grouped into single cases for more efficient triage. What determines how findings are grouped into cases?
column3: Security analysts must manually link related findings to cases using the Security Operations console to group them appropriately.
column4: A custom YARA-L rule must be created in Google SecOps to define the correlation logic for grouping findings into cases.
column5: Findings are grouped based on the time window in which they are detected, with all findings within a 24-hour period placed in the same case.
column6: Findings with the same parameters such as finding type, resource, and resource owner are automatically grouped into one case by the connector.
column8: The SCC Enterprise – Urgent Posture Findings Connector analyzes incoming findings and groups them into new or existing cases based on matching parameters. Multiple findings with the same parameters are grouped into one case, and case priority is determined by the highest severity among all findings in the case. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/cases-overview

column2: Your organization wants to implement a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy that detects when security-critical log data stops being ingested for more than 15 minutes. This could indicate a logging pipeline failure or a malicious attempt to disable logging. What type of alerting policy should you configure?
column3: Configure a metric-absence alerting policy monitoring the log-based metric with a trigger absence time of 15 minutes.
column4: Set up an uptime check monitoring the logging endpoint and create an alerting policy when the check fails.
column5: Create a metric-threshold alerting policy with a condition that fires when the metric value equals zero for 15 minutes.
column6: Configure a log-based alerting policy with a negative filter that triggers when no logs match the criteria.
column8: Metric-absence alerting policies are specifically designed to detect when monitored time series have no data for a specified period. Setting the trigger absence time to 15 minutes will generate an alert when no matching log entries have been received within that window. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/metric-absence

column2: Your organization wants to ensure that attack exposure scores in Security Command Center accurately reflect your business priorities. You need to configure which resources should be considered high-value for attack path simulations. What should you do?
column3: Enable the default high-value resource set and modify the built-in priority values through the Security Command Center API.
column4: Create IAM policies that grant elevated access to critical resources, which Risk Engine automatically detects as high-value indicators.
column5: Configure security marks on individual resources to flag them as high-value and trigger attack path calculations for marked resources.
column6: Create resource value configurations to define your high-value resource set, assigning priority values of HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW to resources that match your criteria.
column8: You must define a high-value resource set through resource value configurations to get attack exposure scores that accurately reflect your security priorities. You can assign priority values (HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW) to resources, and these values influence how Risk Engine calculates attack exposure scores during simulations. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/attack-exposure-learn

column2: Your security team uses Google SecOps for SIEM and has configured Advanced BigQuery Export to access UDM events, rule detections, and IOC matches. An analyst wants to perform custom threat hunting by comparing historical login events with a custom threat intelligence list containing suspicious IP addresses that are not included in Google Threat Intelligence feeds. How should the analyst accomplish this?
column3: Upload the custom threat intelligence list to Google SecOps as a reference list and create an Applied Threat Intelligence feed to enable automatic IOC matching.
column4: Query the secops_linked_data.events table in BigQuery and use a JOIN operation with a BigQuery table containing the custom threat intelligence IP addresses.
column5: Create a custom detection rule in Google SecOps YARA-L that references the external BigQuery table containing the threat intelligence list.
column6: Export the custom threat intelligence list to a CSV file and use the Google SecOps search interface to manually look up each IP address in the UDM search.
column8: Advanced BigQuery Export provides a linked dataset (secops_linked_data) that contains UDM events which can be queried directly in BigQuery. By joining this data with a custom table containing your organization's specific threat intelligence, analysts can hunt for threats that may not be covered by standard GTI feeds. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/bigquery-export

column2: Your threat hunting team receives threat intelligence feeds from multiple external sources through Pub/Sub. Some feeds publish high-priority IOCs that require immediate retrohunt execution, while others contain lower-priority indicators for batch processing. You need to design a Cloud Function-based architecture that processes messages according to their priority without losing any IOCs during processing failures. What should you do?
column3: Deploy separate Cloud Functions for each external feed source with identical retry configurations, store all received IOCs in Cloud Storage before processing, and use a separate orchestration function to prioritize processing order.
column4: Configure a single Pub/Sub topic with message attributes for priority, deploy one Cloud Function that filters messages by priority attribute, and delete low-priority messages after reading to prevent duplicate processing.
column5: Create a Cloud Function that pulls from all topics simultaneously, sorts IOCs by priority in memory, processes high-priority items first, and acknowledges all messages at the end of each function execution.
column6: Create separate Pub/Sub topics for high and low priority feeds, deploy a Cloud Function with concurrent execution for the high-priority topic, configure a dead-letter topic for failed messages, and use Cloud Scheduler to batch process low-priority IOCs.
column8: Separating topics by priority enables different processing behaviors. Cloud Functions with Pub/Sub triggers support retry policies and dead-letter topics for handling failures. This ensures no messages are lost while allowing priority-based processing. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/use-with-cloud-function-triggers

column2: Your organization has deployed Security Command Center Enterprise and is using the SCC Enterprise – Urgent Posture Findings Connector to ingest findings into cases. Security analysts report that the number of cases is overwhelming due to many findings appearing that represent expected behavior or are irrelevant to the organization's security posture. You need to reduce the volume of findings appearing in cases while maintaining audit records. What should you do?
column3: Modify the SCC Enterprise – Urgent Posture Findings Connector to use a more restrictive filter expression to exclude irrelevant finding categories.
column4: Create dynamic mute rules with filters that match the irrelevant findings to prevent them from appearing in cases while maintaining audit logs.
column5: Delete the cases containing irrelevant findings from the Security Operations console to reduce the case queue.
column6: Disable the Security Health Analytics detectors that are generating the irrelevant findings.
column8: Dynamic mute rules automatically apply to both existing and new findings, and muted findings are hidden from cases but continue to be logged for audit and compliance purposes. When you mute findings for cases, you prevent them from appearing in cases, which reduces analyst workload while preserving the audit trail. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-mute-findings

column2: Your security team has identified a potential data exfiltration incident involving a Cloud Storage bucket containing sensitive customer data. You need to investigate which principals accessed the bucket during the incident timeframe and identify patterns of bulk data downloads. Which Cloud Logging query approach should you use to effectively investigate this incident?
column3: Query VPC Flow Logs filtering by destination IP addresses matching Cloud Storage service endpoints to identify volume of data transferred during the incident timeframe.
column4: Query Cloud Audit Logs Data Access logs filtering by resource.type='gcs_bucket' and protoPayload.methodName='storage.objects.get' to identify principals and access patterns during the incident timeframe.
column5: Query Cloud Audit Logs Admin Activity logs filtering by resource.type='gcs_bucket' to identify all operations performed on the bucket during the incident timeframe.
column6: Query Cloud Storage usage logs and export them to BigQuery for analysis to identify access patterns and download volumes during the incident timeframe.
column8: Cloud Audit Logs Data Access logs capture read operations on Cloud Storage objects including storage.objects.get method calls. These logs provide principal information (protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail) and request metadata needed to identify bulk download patterns during a specific timeframe. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/audit-logging

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Premium tier activated at the organization level. You want to suppress Security Health Analytics findings for a specific Cloud SQL instance that has been approved for public access due to a legitimate business requirement. What is the recommended approach?
column3: Delete the Cloud SQL instance from Security Command Center's asset inventory to prevent the finding from being generated.
column4: Create a mute rule in Security Command Center to suppress the PUBLIC_SQL_INSTANCE findings for the specific Cloud SQL instance.
column5: Disable the PUBLIC_SQL_INSTANCE detector entirely in the Security Command Center Services settings.
column6: Apply the security mark allow_public_sql_instance:true to the Cloud SQL instance to exclude it from detection.
column8: For Security Command Center activations on or after June 26, 2023, the mute feature is the recommended method to suppress findings for specific assets. The mute feature allows you to suppress unwanted findings while still allowing the detectors to scan the assets. Security marks for allowlisting are deprecated and will no longer work after April 15, 2025. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-security-health-analytics

column2: Your organization stores Google SecOps UDM events in BigQuery using the managed data lake export. During a threat hunt, you need to identify all network connections to IP addresses that match IOCs from your threat intelligence feeds. Which BigQuery table should you query to find these matches?
column3: The ioc_matches table in the Google SecOps datalake dataset.
column4: The udm_events_aggregates table with a JOIN to an external IOC reference table.
column5: The rule_detections table filtered by IOC-related rule names.
column6: The entity_graph table with a filter on network entity relationships.
column8: The Google SecOps datalake dataset in BigQuery includes an ioc_matches table that specifically stores IOC matches found against UDM events. This table contains artifacts such as domains and IP addresses from events that match Indicator of Compromise feeds. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/overview-chronicle-bigquery

column2: During an active security incident, your incident response team needs to isolate a compromised VM while simultaneously allowing your forensics team to access it from a dedicated forensics VPC. The forensics VPC is already peered with the production VPC. You need to implement this containment strategy. What should you do?
column3: Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter with an ingress rule allowing only the forensics service account, then add the compromised VM's project to the perimeter.
column4: Remove all existing network tags from the compromised VM and add a quarantine tag, then modify existing allow rules to exclude the quarantine tag.
column5: Tag the compromised VM with an isolation tag, create a deny-all ingress rule with priority 100 targeting the tag, and create an allow ingress rule with priority 50 for the forensics subnet CIDR range.
column6: Move the compromised VM to an isolated subnet with no routes to the internet, then configure IAP tunneling for forensics team access.
column8: Firewall rules are evaluated by priority (lower number = higher priority). By creating a deny-all rule at priority 100 and an allow rule at priority 50 for the forensics subnet, you effectively block all traffic except from the forensics team. The unique tag ensures only the compromised VM is affected. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls

column2: Your organization is investigating a potential security incident that occurred two weeks ago. You need to copy relevant Cloud Audit Logs from your project's _Default log bucket to a Cloud Storage bucket for forensic analysis and preservation. The log bucket does not have CMEK configured. What should you do?
column3: Use the gcloud logging copy command to retroactively copy log entries from the _Default log bucket to the Cloud Storage bucket.
column4: Create a new log sink with an inclusion filter for Cloud Audit Logs and set the destination to the Cloud Storage bucket.
column5: Export logs directly from Logs Explorer by selecting all relevant entries and downloading them to Cloud Storage.
column6: Use BigQuery to query the linked dataset from the log bucket and export query results to Cloud Storage.
column8: Cloud Logging supports copying log entries from log buckets to Cloud Storage buckets using the gcloud logging copy command. This allows you to retroactively export historical logs for forensic analysis. The operation works on buckets without CMEK configured. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/routing/copy-logs

column2: Detection engineering"Your security operations team uses Google Security Operations (SecOps) and has identified a new threat actor's techniques through threat intelligence research. You want to search your historical event data to determine if your environment was previously compromised by this threat actor. Which Google SecOps capability should you use?
column3: Run a retrohunt using a YARA-L detection rule that defines the threat actor's techniques, specifying a historical time range to scan existing event data for matches.
column4: Export all historical logs to BigQuery and execute SQL queries that implement the detection logic against the exported dataset.
column5: Configure a composite detection rule that correlates current alerts with historical entity context from the entity graph to identify prior compromise indicators.
column6: Enable the detection rule as a live rule and wait for the Detection Engine to process historical backlogs automatically against newly created rules.
column8: Retrohunt allows you to run a YARA-L rule against historical data stored in Google SecOps to search for detections throughout existing data. This enables security teams to hunt for indicators of past compromise using newly developed detection logic against the full retention period of event data. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Your security team is conducting threat hunting across your Google Cloud environment and suspects that an attacker may be performing network reconnaissance by conducting port scans from a compromised VM. You want to write a BigQuery query against VPC Flow Logs to identify potential port scanning activity. Which query criteria should you use to identify this behavior?
column3: Query for source IP addresses with a high count of distinct destination port values and a low packet count per connection, filtering for traffic where the source is internal and connection durations are brief.
column4: Query for destination IP addresses receiving traffic from external sources on well-known ports like 22 and 443, filtering for high byte counts to identify data exfiltration attempts.
column5: Query for traffic patterns where the same 5-tuple appears repeatedly with consistent packet sizes, indicating automated scanning tools are being used across the network.
column6: Query for any traffic originating from external IP addresses that was blocked by firewall rules, as port scanners always originate from external networks.
column8: Port scanning typically involves a single source IP attempting connections to many different destination ports on one or more targets, with minimal data transfer and brief connection attempts. Low packet counts with high distinct port counts indicate scanning behavior rather than legitimate application traffic. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/flow-logs

column2: Your security team is overwhelmed by the number of vulnerability findings in Security Command Center. You need to prioritize remediation based on which vulnerabilities pose the greatest risk to your critical business systems. What is the most effective approach to configure SCC for vulnerability prioritization?
column3: Sort all vulnerability findings by severity level and address Critical findings first regardless of affected resources.
column4: Export findings to BigQuery and run SQL queries to count findings per resource to identify the most vulnerable assets.
column5: Create custom dashboards in Looker Studio to visualize all findings and manually prioritize based on affected resource names.
column6: Define a high-value resource set by creating resource value configurations, then prioritize findings based on attack exposure scores.
column8: Attack exposure scores measure how much a detected security issue exposes high-value resources to potential cyberattacks. To get scores that accurately reflect your security priorities, you must define your high-value resource set using resource value configurations. Findings with higher scores should receive higher remediation priority. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/attack-exposure-learn

column2: Your security team has identified that a service account in Project A has permissions to impersonate service accounts in Project B, creating a potential lateral movement risk. You want to identify all such cross-project impersonation scenarios in your organization and receive recommendations to remediate them. What should you do?
column3: Enable VPC Service Controls to restrict which projects can access service accounts and prevent cross-project impersonation.
column4: Use IAM Recommender to review lateral movement insights and associated role recommendations for service accounts across projects.
column5: Configure Cloud Audit Logs to track all service account impersonation events and manually analyze the logs to identify cross-project access patterns.
column6: Create a custom YARA-L detection rule in Google SecOps to detect service account impersonation activities across projects.
column8: IAM Recommender generates lateral movement insights that identify roles allowing service accounts in one project to impersonate service accounts in another project. These insights highlight impersonation abilities and whether permissions were used in the last 90 days, helping you understand and remediate cross-project risks. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/policy-intelligence/docs/role-recommendations-overview

column2: Detection engineering"You are developing detection rules in Google Security Operations (SecOps) SIEM and need to identify when entities exceed risk thresholds. You want to create a YARA-L rule that triggers alerts based on changes to an entity's risk score without requiring any specific ingested event to occur. Which approach should you use?
column3: Create a multi-event rule that correlates all detection events for an entity and calculates the cumulative risk score in the outcome section.
column4: Use entity context data in a single-event rule with conditions on the graph.risk_score.normalized_risk_score field.
column5: Create a YARA-L rule using the ENTITY_RISK_CHANGE UDM event type to trigger independently of ingested events when entity risk scores change.
column6: Configure the Risk Analytics dashboard alerts to send notifications when entity risk scores exceed thresholds.
column8: The ENTITY_RISK_CHANGE UDM event type allows you to write YARA-L detection rules that trigger independently of ingested events and focus specifically on changes in an entity's risk score. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/release-notes

column2: You are configuring a Cloud Logging sink to export security-relevant logs to Cloud Storage for long-term retention and later analysis in Google Security Operations. You need to include Admin Activity audit logs, Data Access audit logs, and VPC Flow Logs in the export. Which sink filter should you configure?
column3: logName=projects/*/logs/cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Factivity OR logName=projects/*/logs/cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Fdata_access
column4: protoPayload.@type=type.googleapis.com/google.cloud.audit.AuditLog AND resource.type=gce_subnetwork
column5: logName:cloudaudit.googleapis.com OR resource.type=gce_subnetwork
column6: severity>=INFO AND (logName:audit OR resource.type:vpc)
column8: This filter captures both Cloud Audit Logs (which include Admin Activity and Data Access audit logs via the cloudaudit.googleapis.com log name pattern) and VPC Flow Logs (which use the gce_subnetwork resource type). The logName field with the colon operator performs a substring match, capturing all audit log types. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/configure_export_v2

column2: Your organization has enabled Web Security Scanner managed scans in Security Command Center at the organization level. After reviewing the findings, you notice that some critical applications are not being scanned. You need to understand the limitations and ensure comprehensive coverage of your web applications. Which limitation explains why some applications might not be scanned by managed scans?
column3: Managed scans only run during maintenance windows specified in the project configuration.
column4: Managed scans only support applications using default ports 80 for HTTP and 443 for HTTPS connections.
column5: Managed scans require explicit authentication credentials to be configured for each application.
column6: Managed scans are limited to applications deployed in specific Google Cloud regions.
column8: Web Security Scanner managed scans support only applications that use the default port, which is 80 for HTTP connections and 443 for HTTPS connections. If your application uses a non-default port, you must configure a custom scan instead. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-web-security-scanner-overview

column2: Your organization deployed a critical security log ingestion service on Google Cloud. You configured a service-level objective (SLO) with a 99.5% availability target measured over a 30-day rolling compliance period. Security leadership requests a centralized view showing whether the security service is meeting its SLO. You need to create a dashboard to visualize the SLO performance. What should you do?
column3: Create a line chart using the service's availability metric and manually add a threshold line at 99.5% to represent the SLO target.
column4: Add an SLO widget to a custom dashboard and configure it to display the error budget metric for the security log ingestion service.
column5: Export SLO metrics to BigQuery and use Looker Studio to create a compliance visualization that updates weekly.
column6: Configure a scorecard widget to display the average availability percentage and set color thresholds at 99.5% for visual indication.
column8: Adding an SLO widget allows you to view the health, compliance, or error budget of a service-level objective. By displaying error budget, security leadership can see the remaining tolerance for failures before violating the SLO. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/dashboards/slos

column2: You are building an investigation playbook in Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR that requires a senior analyst to approve a containment action before the system isolates a compromised endpoint. You want to ensure the approval step has a deadline and the playbook handles situations where the analyst does not respond in time. What should you do?
column3: Add a parallel branch that executes the containment automatically while simultaneously sending a notification to the senior analyst for awareness.
column4: Configure the containment action as Automatic type with a pre-approval flag that requires the senior analyst to have previously authorized this action type.
column5: Configure the containment action as Manual type, assign it to a SOC role, enable Time to respond with a deadline, and add an 'If previous Step failed' condition to control the alternative flow.
column6: Create a separate approval workflow playbook that sends an email to the analyst and polls for a response using a loop action with timeout.
column8: Manual actions pause the playbook until user input is received. The Time to respond setting enforces a deadline, and if the analyst does not respond in time, the action fails. Using 'If previous Step failed' conditional step allows the playbook to handle timeout scenarios by branching to an alternative flow. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/assign-actions-and-playbook-blocks

column2: Your security team is performing threat hunting to identify potential privilege escalation attempts in your Google Cloud environment. You need to detect when IAM permissions are granted over service accounts that could allow impersonation or key creation. Which approach should you use to efficiently analyze this activity at scale?
column3: Configure Cloud Monitoring alerts on all Data Access audit logs to trigger when any service account authentication event occurs across the organization.
column4: Use Logs Explorer to manually review Policy Denied audit logs for rejected access attempts to service account resources across each project individually.
column5: Use Log Analytics with SQL queries to analyze Admin Activity audit logs for SetIamPolicy operations that grant iam.serviceAccountKeys.create or iam.serviceAccounts.actAs permissions.
column6: Export all System Event audit logs to BigQuery and create scheduled queries to identify any automated Google Cloud system operations related to service accounts.
column8: Log Analytics allows you to use BigQuery-standard SQL to query and aggregate audit logs at scale. Admin Activity audit logs record IAM policy changes, and analyzing SetIamPolicy operations for service account permissions is the most effective way to detect privilege escalation risks involving impersonation or key creation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/analyze-audit-logs

column2: You need to enable your security team to run SQL queries against Cloud Logging data using BigQuery Studio while maintaining the lowest operational overhead. The logs are currently stored in a Cloud Logging log bucket. What configuration steps should you complete?
column3: Upgrade the log bucket to use Log Analytics, then create a linked BigQuery dataset from the log bucket.
column4: Enable the BigQuery API and create scheduled queries to export log summaries to BigQuery tables on a daily basis.
column5: Configure the log bucket with CMEK encryption and grant the security team the Logs Viewer role to query logs in BigQuery.
column6: Create a log sink to route logs directly to a BigQuery dataset, then query the routed logs in BigQuery.
column8: Upgrading the log bucket to use Log Analytics enables SQL querying capabilities, and creating a linked BigQuery dataset allows BigQuery services to read the log data directly. This configuration lets you query logs from BigQuery Studio, Looker Studio, or the bq command-line tool without needing to manage separate data pipelines or storage. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/log-analytics

column2: Your security team needs to identify entities with the highest risk in your environment and monitor their behavior over time. The team wants to view entity risk scores, track findings trends, and create watchlists for high-value targets. Which Google Security Operations (SecOps) SIEM feature should you use?
column3: Context Aware Detections - Risk dashboard with detection rules configuration.
column4: Risk Analytics dashboard with Behavioral Analytics section and Watchlists tab.
column5: Cloud Detection and Response dashboard with CDIR Rulesets Enabled visualization.
column6: Main dashboard with Global Threat Map - IoC IP Matches visualization.
column8: The Risk Analytics dashboard provides entity risk visualization with a Behavioral Analytics section listing entities by risk scores and a Watchlists section for tracking specific entities. It includes a Findings timeline chart tracking risk scores over time and supports configuring up to 200 watchlists. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/risk-analytics-dashboard

column2: Your organization is exporting Cloud Audit Logs from multiple projects to a centralized BigQuery dataset for security analysis. After several weeks of operation, you discover that some log entries are being written to a table named 'export_errors' instead of the expected destination tables. You need to identify the root cause and prevent this issue from recurring. What is the most likely cause of this issue?
column3: The BigQuery dataset's storage quota has been exceeded, causing logs to be redirected to the error table.
column4: The Cloud Logging sink filter is misconfigured and matches logs with incompatible resource types for the destination table.
column5: A later log entry has a field type that differs from the field type established by the first log entry that created the table schema.
column6: The sink's writer identity service account was revoked from the BigQuery Data Editor role on the destination dataset.
column8: When Cloud Logging exports to BigQuery, the first log entry received determines the schema. A schema mismatch occurs when later log entries change the field type for an existing field. BigQuery then writes the mismatched entries to an export_errors table rather than the original destination table. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/bigquery

column2: Your security team is investigating a VPC Service Controls access denial for a legitimate service account attempting to access Cloud Storage resources within a protected perimeter. You need to determine the root cause and resolve the issue quickly. What is the most effective approach?
column3: Review the perimeter's restricted services list and remove Cloud Storage temporarily for testing.
column4: Use the VPC Service Controls troubleshooter in the Google Cloud console with the unique ID from the audit log to analyze the denial.
column5: Create an access level with the service account identity and apply it to the perimeter.
column6: Export the Cloud Audit Logs to BigQuery and query for all VPC Service Controls violations in the past 30 days.
column8: The VPC Service Controls troubleshooter provides detailed analysis of access denial events using the unique ID logged in Cloud Audit Logs. It evaluates the denial against all perimeter configurations and provides specific remediation guidance. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/troubleshooter

column2: Your security team has received a list of malicious IP addresses from a threat intelligence feed. You need to search for these IOCs across 90 days of historical network logs stored in a Log Analytics-enabled bucket. You want to minimize query costs while efficiently matching the IOCs. What should you do?
column3: Query the logs directly in Logs Explorer using advanced filter syntax with each IP address listed in an OR statement for the full 90-day range.
column4: Configure a log-based metric for each malicious IP address and create alerting policies to detect historical matches in Cloud Monitoring dashboards.
column5: Export the logs to Cloud Storage, import them into a new BigQuery dataset, and run a CONTAINS query against all IP address fields in the entire dataset.
column6: Create a linked BigQuery dataset from the log bucket, load the IOC list into a separate BigQuery table, and use a JOIN query with partition filters on the timestamp column.
column8: Creating a linked dataset allows BigQuery to read log data directly without data movement. Loading IOCs into a reference table enables efficient JOIN operations, and using partition filters reduces query costs by limiting data scanned. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/query-linked-dataset

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Premium tier and needs to test whether Event Threat Detection is properly configured to generate findings. You want to verify the configuration without waiting for actual threats to occur. What is the recommended approach?
column3: Wait for Event Threat Detection to perform its scheduled daily scan and review the scan completion logs for verification.
column4: Review the Event Threat Detection service status in the Security Command Center console to confirm the service is enabled and healthy.
column5: Create a custom module that monitors for a test event pattern and use it to validate that findings are properly generated.
column6: Intentionally trigger a detector by performing an action that matches the detector's criteria, such as creating a test IAM policy with suspicious characteristics.
column8: Google Cloud documentation recommends intentionally triggering detectors to verify Event Threat Detection configuration. By performing actions that match detector criteria, you can generate test findings and confirm that Event Threat Detection is working correctly. Detection latencies are generally less than 15 minutes. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-event-threat-detection

column2: Your organization's security team has identified a potential lateral movement attack where service accounts in one project may have been used to impersonate service accounts in other projects. You need to proactively identify which service accounts have cross-project impersonation capabilities to assess the blast radius. What should you do?
column3: Use IAM Policy Analyzer to query for all principals with roles/iam.serviceAccountUser at the organization level and export results to BigQuery for analysis.
column4: Review lateral movement insights in IAM Recommender to identify service accounts with impersonation permissions across projects, then correlate with permission usage data from the last 90 days.
column5: Query Cloud Audit Logs for all GenerateAccessToken and SignBlob method calls across your organization to trace service account impersonation chains.
column6: Enable Data Access audit logs for IAM across all projects and create a log-based alert for any service account token generation events.
column8: Lateral movement insights identify roles that allow service accounts in one project to impersonate service accounts in another project. These insights include information about which service accounts can be impersonated and whether impersonation permissions were used in the last 90 days, providing actionable data for assessing the lateral movement risk. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/policy-intelligence/docs/lateral-movement-insights

column2: You are configuring security alerting for your Google Cloud environment and need to choose the appropriate alerting approach. You want to detect complex patterns across multiple log entries, such as identifying when the same source IP has accessed more than 5 different sensitive resources within 10 minutes. The detection must run continuously without manual intervention. Which alerting approach should you use?
column3: Create a log-based alerting policy that matches on resource access events.
column4: Create multiple log-based counter metrics with labels for source IP and resource, then create an alerting policy using metric ratios.
column5: Create a SQL-based alerting policy in Log Analytics with a query that aggregates access events by source IP and counts distinct resources accessed.
column6: Schedule a Cloud Function to run Log Analytics queries every 10 minutes and send alerts via Pub/Sub.
column8: SQL-based alerting policies are effective for detecting complex patterns in log entries or aggregations of log data that cannot be evaluated by log-based alerting policies. These policies run automatically on a schedule and can use SQL aggregation functions like COUNT DISTINCT with GROUP BY to identify the pattern. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/sql-in-alerting

column2: Your organization wants to use Cloud Logging to detect security events using SQL queries that identify patterns across aggregated audit logs over time. You need to configure the infrastructure to enable SQL-based security analysis while minimizing costs. What should you do?
column3: Export logs to Cloud Storage buckets and use BigQuery external tables to query the exported data for security analysis.
column4: Upgrade an existing log bucket to use Log Analytics and create a linked BigQuery dataset to enable SQL queries against log data.
column5: Configure log-based alerting policies to monitor individual audit log entries for security events using filter expressions.
column6: Create a new log sink that routes all audit logs directly to a BigQuery dataset, then write SQL queries against the BigQuery tables.
column8: Upgrading a log bucket to use Log Analytics enables SQL querying through the Log Analytics page. Creating a linked BigQuery dataset provides read access to log data without incurring BigQuery ingestion or storage costs, as Logging still stores the data while BigQuery can read it. This approach supports running Community Security Analytics (CSA) queries for threat detection. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/buckets

column2: Your security team needs to analyze historical logs in BigQuery to search for IOCs (Indicators of Compromise) such as malicious IP addresses and domains that were recently published by your threat intelligence provider. The team wants to match the IOCs against Cloud Logging audit logs that have been routed to BigQuery. What approach should you use to efficiently identify matches between the IOCs and your logs?
column3: Create a BigQuery table containing the IOCs, and use a SQL JOIN query between the IOCs table and your routed audit logs to identify matching IP addresses and domains.
column4: Export the IOCs to a CSV file and manually search through Cloud Logging Logs Explorer using filter expressions for each indicator individually.
column5: Configure Google SecOps Applied Threat Intelligence feeds to automatically match IOCs against logs stored exclusively in BigQuery through direct feed integration.
column6: Use BigQuery's ML.DETECT_ANOMALIES function with your IOC list as the training dataset to automatically detect matching indicators in the logs.
column8: BigQuery supports efficient JOIN operations between tables, allowing you to load your IOCs into a separate table and join them against the routed audit log tables. This approach is scalable for large volumes of logs and allows you to match multiple IOC types (IPs, domains, hashes) against corresponding fields in your logs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax

column2: Your security operations team needs to monitor and audit when Google personnel access customer data in your Google Cloud environment. You want to integrate this visibility into your existing SIEM tooling for compliance and auditing purposes. Which log type should you ingest into Google Security Operations (SecOps)?
column3: Admin Activity audit logs
column4: Cloud Audit Logs only
column5: Access Transparency logs
column6: Security Command Center findings
column8: Access Transparency logs record actions taken by Google personnel when accessing customer data. They include details such as affected resources, time of action, reasons for access, and accessor location. These logs can be integrated with SIEM tools for compliance auditing. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/access-transparency/docs/overview

column2: Your security team has received a threat intelligence feed containing a list of 50 suspicious IP addresses that have been involved in recent attacks targeting cloud environments. You need to configure Event Threat Detection to generate findings when any resource in your Google Cloud organization connects to these IP addresses. What should you do?
column3: Create a Cloud Logging log-based metric that triggers an alert when VPC Flow Logs show connections to the specified IP addresses, then export findings to SCC.
column4: Enable the built-in Malware: Bad IP detector and add the custom IP addresses to Google's threat intelligence database using a support request.
column5: Create a Configurable Bad IP custom module using a JSON template that includes the IP addresses in the 'ips' parameter and ensure VPC Flow Logs are enabled.
column6: Create a Security Health Analytics custom module with CEL expressions to detect network connections to the specified IP addresses from Cloud Audit Logs.
column8: The Configurable Bad IP custom module is specifically designed for detecting connections to custom suspicious IP addresses. The module requires a JSON template with the 'ips' parameter containing the list of addresses, and VPC Flow Logs must be enabled to detect network connections. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: You are deploying a new organization policy constraint to restrict resource locations across your Google Cloud organization. The constraint will deny resource creation in non-approved regions. Before enforcing this policy in production, you want to assess the potential impact and identify which existing workflows would be affected without blocking any operations. What should you do?
column3: Create the organization policy in dry-run mode and review the audit logs for violations.
column4: Configure the organization policy with inheritFromParent set to false on all child resources to prevent enforcement.
column5: Apply the constraint at the folder level first, then gradually move it to the organization level after validation.
column6: Use Policy Simulator to test the constraint and immediately enforce the policy at the organization level.
column8: An organization policy in dry-run mode allows violations to be audit-logged without being denied. This enables you to monitor how the policy change would impact your workflows before enforcing it in production. You can review the dry-run logs to identify potential violations before setting the live policy. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/dry-run-policy

column2: Your security team is investigating a potential privilege escalation incident where a user may have modified IAM policies to grant themselves elevated permissions on sensitive resources. You need to identify all IAM policy changes made by this specific user across your Google Cloud organization within the last 24 hours. Which Logs Explorer query filter should you use to retrieve this information?
column3: protoPayload.methodName='SetIamPolicy' AND protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail='suspect-user@example.com'
column4: protoPayload.methodName='GetIamPolicy' AND protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail='suspect-user@example.com'
column5: protoPayload.authorizationInfo.permission='iam.serviceAccounts.actAs' AND protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail='suspect-user@example.com'
column6: protoPayload.serviceName='iam.googleapis.com' AND protoPayload.request.member='user:suspect-user@example.com'
column8: SetIamPolicy operations are recorded in Admin Activity audit logs, and the authenticationInfo.principalEmail field identifies the principal who performed the action. This filter will return all IAM policy modifications made by the specified user. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit/understanding-audit-logs

column2: Your security team is configuring Event Threat Detection custom modules to detect connections to suspicious domains from your organization's threat intelligence. The module requires Cloud DNS logs. After deploying the custom module, no findings are generated despite known test traffic. What is the most likely cause of this issue?
column3: The custom module quota of 200 findings per parent resource per hour has been exceeded.
column4: The custom module JSON configuration file exceeds the 6 MB size limit.
column5: Cloud DNS logging is not enabled for the VPC network, and the custom module has no logs to scan.
column6: Event Threat Detection is only available with organization-level activation and cannot scan project-level logs.
column8: Event Threat Detection custom modules require specific log types to be enabled. For domain-based detection, Cloud DNS logs must be enabled in the VPC. After you enable Event Threat Detection, it generates findings by scanning specific logs, and some logs are turned off by default. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-event-threat-detection

column2: Your organization maintains a list of known malicious IP addresses from an internal threat intelligence team. You need to configure Event Threat Detection to generate findings when VPC resources connect to these IP addresses. You want to define custom severity levels and remediation guidance for your security team. What should you do?
column3: Create a Configurable Bad IP custom module using a JSON template that includes your IP list, severity level, description, and recommendation parameters.
column4: Configure a Cloud Armor security policy with your malicious IP list and integrate it with Event Threat Detection for automatic findings.
column5: Enable the built-in Malware: Bad IP detector and upload your threat intelligence feed directly to Security Command Center.
column6: Create a custom detection rule in Google SecOps SIEM using YARA-L and export the findings to Security Command Center.
column8: The Configurable Bad IP custom module allows you to specify your own list of suspicious IP addresses and customize the metadata including severity, description, and remediation recommendations. Custom module templates are written in JSON and let you define detection parameters that control what events in log entries should trigger findings. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: Your security team is investigating a critical toxic combination finding detected by Security Command Center Risk Engine. The finding shows a high attack exposure score and affects a resource path leading to your high-value BigQuery dataset. What does this toxic combination represent and how should you respond?
column3: A group of security issues that together create an attack path to your high-value resource; remediate the contributing issues to eliminate the attack path.
column4: A false positive detection caused by misconfigured scanning parameters; mute the finding and adjust the Risk Engine settings.
column5: A threat finding indicating active compromise of your BigQuery dataset; immediately isolate the affected resources and initiate incident response.
column6: A single critical vulnerability with multiple CVEs; apply the vendor-provided patch to remediate all associated vulnerabilities.
column8: Toxic combinations represent groups of security issues that, when they occur together in a particular pattern, create a path that an attacker could use to reach and compromise high-value resources. Each toxic combination has an attack exposure score reflecting its risk. Remediation involves addressing the contributing security issues to break the attack path. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/toxic-combinations-overview

column2: Your security team wants to implement automated remediation for Security Command Center findings. When a Security Health Analytics detector identifies an OPEN_FIREWALL finding, a Cloud Function should automatically update the firewall rule to restrict access. You need to configure the event-driven architecture that connects SCC findings to Cloud Functions. What should you do?
column3: Create a NotificationConfig with a filter for OPEN_FIREWALL findings to publish to a Pub/Sub topic, and deploy a Cloud Function with a Pub/Sub trigger subscribed to that topic.
column4: Enable continuous exports to BigQuery and use scheduled queries to trigger Cloud Functions for OPEN_FIREWALL remediation.
column5: Configure Event Threat Detection to directly invoke the Cloud Function when OPEN_FIREWALL findings are detected using an HTTP trigger.
column6: Create a Cloud Asset Inventory feed to monitor firewall changes and trigger Cloud Functions to remediate findings directly from asset updates.
column8: The Security Command Center Notifications API uses NotificationConfig to export findings to Pub/Sub topics in near-real time. Cloud Functions can then be triggered by Pub/Sub messages to perform automated remediation actions. The filter ensures only relevant findings trigger the function. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-notifications

column2: You are managing case workflows in Security Command Center Enterprise. Multiple Security Health Analytics findings with different severity levels have been grouped into a single case. You need to understand how case priority is determined when findings have varying severities. Which statement correctly describes the case priority assignment behavior?
column3: Case priority is automatically set based on the highest finding severity among all findings in the case, and updates automatically when finding severity changes.
column4: Case priority is calculated as an average of all finding severities in the case, weighted by the number of findings at each severity level.
column5: Case priority is set to the severity of the first finding ingested and remains static unless manually updated by an analyst.
column6: Muted findings are excluded from case priority calculations, and only active unmuted findings determine the case priority.
column8: Case priority is based on the highest finding severity. When the finding severity changes, Security Command Center automatically updates the case priority to match the highest severity property among all findings in the case. This ensures cases are prioritized appropriately based on the most critical finding they contain. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/cases-overview

column2: Platform operations"Your organization has configured a Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR environment where multiple phishing response playbooks may match incoming email alerts. You need to ensure that only the most specific playbook executes automatically and that additional playbooks can be attached manually if needed. What configuration should you implement?
column3: Use environment-specific playbook configurations to separate playbooks by alert source and prevent multiple playbook matches.
column4: Configure all phishing playbooks with the same priority and use Custom Trigger conditions to ensure only one matches each alert.
column5: Set playbook priority values between 1 and 3, with the most specific playbook at priority 1, and attach additional playbooks manually as needed up to the maximum limit.
column6: Create a master orchestrator playbook that evaluates conditions and calls other playbooks as nested sub-playbooks based on alert attributes.
column8: You can set playbook priority between 1 (highest) and 3 (lowest), and only one playbook can attach automatically based on priority. An additional nine playbooks can be attached manually, for a total of 10 playbooks per alert. This allows the most specific playbook to execute first while permitting manual attachment of others. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/attaching-playbooks-to-an-alert

column2: Your organization uses Google Security Operations (SecOps) and needs to integrate threat intelligence capabilities for IOC correlation and enrichment. Your security team requires access to the broadest range of threat intelligence features, including Mandiant frontline intelligence, crowdsourced community data, and deep dark web monitoring. Which integration should you configure to meet these requirements?
column3: Configure the VirusTotal integration with Premium API access to unlock Mandiant intelligence and dark web monitoring features.
column4: Configure the Google Threat Intelligence (GTI) integration, which combines VirusTotal capabilities with Mandiant intelligence and Google threat insights.
column5: Configure the VirusTotal v3 integration to access the full VirusTotal database including Mandiant intelligence feeds and dark web monitoring capabilities.
column6: Configure both VirusTotal v2 and Mandiant Threat Intelligence integrations separately to achieve the combined functionality.
column8: Google Threat Intelligence unifies VirusTotal's advanced capabilities with Mandiant's leading threat activity insights, providing automated context, enrichment, and alerting. It includes features like deep dark web monitoring and comprehensive IOC analysis that VirusTotal alone does not provide. Google documentation recommends using GTI over VirusTotal integration as it provides more capabilities and features. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security/products/threat-intelligence

column2: Your organization wants to prevent default service accounts from being automatically granted the Editor role in new Google Cloud projects. You also need to ensure that existing default service accounts retain their current permissions during the transition. What should you do?
column3: Apply the constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountCreation organization policy constraint to prevent new service accounts from being created.
column4: Configure a Cloud Function triggered by new project creation events to automatically remove the Editor role from default service accounts.
column5: Apply the constraints/iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts organization policy constraint at the organization level.
column6: Delete all default service accounts across existing projects and create custom service accounts with minimal permissions.
column8: This constraint prevents default service accounts in new projects from automatically receiving the Editor role. Applying the constraint does not remove the Editor role from existing default service accounts, allowing for a gradual transition. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-service-accounts

column2: You are configuring an Event Threat Detection custom module using the gcloud CLI to detect connections to malicious IP addresses from your organization's threat intelligence feed. You need to define the severity and remediation guidance for findings generated by this module. Which component of the JSON template should you configure?
column3: The sourceProperties section, including detectionPriority and remediationSteps fields.
column4: The finding_config section, including risk_level and next_steps fields.
column5: The detection_parameters section, including alert_severity and mitigation_steps fields.
column6: The metadata section, including severity, description, and recommendation fields.
column8: The metadata section of the custom module JSON template contains the severity level (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, or CRITICAL), description of the custom module, and recommendation field for remediation guidance. These parameters help security teams understand and respond to findings. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/use-custom-modules-etd

column2: During an active security incident, your incident response team identifies that a service account has been compromised and is being used to exfiltrate data. You need to immediately stop the malicious activity while preserving the ability to investigate and potentially restore the service account if the detection was a false positive. What is the most appropriate IAM action to take?
column3: Remove all IAM role bindings from the service account at the project level.
column4: Disable all service account keys using the gcloud iam service-accounts keys disable command.
column5: Disable the service account using the gcloud iam service-accounts disable command.
column6: Delete the service account using the gcloud iam service-accounts delete command.
column8: Disabling a service account immediately revokes its ability to authenticate and access resources, but it can be re-enabled later if the detection is determined to be a false positive. This approach balances immediate containment with investigative flexibility. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-accounts-disable-enable

column2: Security Command Center Enterprise has detected several Security Health Analytics findings for misconfigurations in your Google Cloud environment. You notice that findings with the same parameters are grouped into a single case. An analyst wants to mute all findings in a case that represent acceptable configurations. The analyst runs the Update Finding manual action on the case. What happens when all findings in the case are successfully muted?
column3: The case is archived and the associated Jira or ServiceNow ticket is automatically deleted from the ticketing system.
column4: The case remains open but is moved to a 'Muted' status queue for periodic review by security administrators.
column5: The case stays open and the muted findings remain as alerts but are marked with a 'Muted' label for visibility.
column6: Security Command Center automatically closes the case since all findings within it are muted.
column8: When you mute all findings in a case, Security Command Center automatically closes the case. Muting findings prevents them from appearing in cases and reduces analyst workload. You can mute findings in bulk by running a manual action on a case using the Update Finding action from the GoogleSecurityCommandCenter integration. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/mute-findings-in-cases

column2: Your organization needs to maintain a comprehensive inventory of all Google Cloud assets across multiple projects for security auditing and compliance purposes. You want to query asset metadata using SQL syntax and enable security analysts to identify resources with overly permissive IAM policies. Which approach should you use?
column3: Export Cloud Asset Inventory data to BigQuery with the IAM_POLICY content type, then run SQL queries on the exported table.
column4: Configure Security Health Analytics to scan for IAM policy violations and export the misconfiguration findings to BigQuery.
column5: Use Security Command Center API to list all assets and export findings to Cloud Storage for analysis using Cloud Data Studio.
column6: Create a custom script using individual service APIs (Compute Engine, Cloud Storage, BigQuery) to collect and aggregate asset data into a centralized database.
column8: Cloud Asset Inventory can export asset metadata directly to BigQuery, and specifying the IAM_POLICY content type includes the IAM bindings on resources. This enables SQL-based analysis of permissions across the organization. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/export-bigquery

column2: Your organization is implementing Google Cloud's Sensitive Data Protection to establish a data classification baseline for your security operations team. You need to configure the discovery service to continuously monitor BigQuery tables across your organization and provide asset context that can inform incident response prioritization. What should you do first?
column3: Enable Cloud Asset Inventory and configure it to export DLP findings from individual inspection jobs to a central BigQuery dataset.
column4: Create a discovery scan configuration at the organization level that defines the scope, inspection templates, and actions for profiling BigQuery data assets.
column5: Submit a request to Google Cloud Support to enable organization-wide DLP scanning with predefined classification policies.
column6: Configure the DLP API to run content.inspect requests on each BigQuery table using a service account with BigQuery Data Viewer permissions.
column8: The discovery service requires a scan configuration that specifies the profiling scope (organization, folder, or project), inspection templates that define which infoTypes to scan for, and actions to take when profiles are generated. This configuration enables continuous monitoring and generates data profiles containing sensitivity and risk levels that provide valuable asset context. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/data-profiles

column2: Your threat hunting team is investigating suspicious lateral movement patterns across your multi-cloud environment using Google Security Operations (SecOps). You need to correlate events showing an initial cloud IAM authentication failure followed by a successful authentication from the same identity within 30 minutes, and then network connection attempts to multiple internal services. Which detection approach should you implement?
column3: Build separate single-event rules for each activity type and use a composite detection rule to correlate the output detections across a 30-minute window.
column4: Create a multi-event YARA-L rule with a 30-minute match window that correlates authentication and network events using the principal identity field.
column5: Configure Event Threat Detection custom detectors in Security Command Center to identify this multi-stage attack pattern across cloud environments.
column6: Create a UDM Search statistical query grouped by user identity with a 30-minute time window to identify the pattern and save it as a dashboard widget.
column8: Multi-event YARA-L rules support correlation across different event types within a specified time window. Using the match section with the principal identity field enables tracking sequential behavior patterns like authentication failures, successful logins, and subsequent network activity from the same identity. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/yara-l-2-0-overview

column2: Your detection engineering team is investigating Web Security Scanner findings in Security Command Center. A SERVER_SIDE_REQUEST_FORGERY finding was detected in one of your Compute Engine web applications. You need to analyze the finding and determine the appropriate remediation. What should you do?
column3: Run an additional custom scan with the LOW risk level setting to verify if the SSRF finding is a false positive before taking remediation action.
column4: Set the finding state to INACTIVE in Security Command Center and create a mute rule to suppress similar findings from appearing.
column5: Review the finding details in Security Command Center to identify the vulnerable URL and implement an allowlist to restrict domains and IP addresses the application can access.
column6: Configure Cloud Armor security policies to block all incoming requests containing SSRF attack patterns in request parameters.
column8: SERVER_SIDE_REQUEST_FORGERY findings indicate the application is vulnerable to SSRF attacks where attackers can make the server perform unauthorized requests. The recommended remediation is to implement an allowlist to limit the domains and IP addresses that the web application can make requests to. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-remediate-web-security-scanner-findings

column2: Your security operations team is building a Looker Studio dashboard to monitor Security Command Center findings streamed to BigQuery. The dashboard will be displayed continuously in the SOC on a wall-mounted screen. The team requires the dashboard to automatically update at least every 15 minutes without manual intervention. How should you configure the dashboard to meet this requirement?
column3: Configure the BigQuery data source data freshness setting to 15 minutes and the dashboard will automatically refresh.
column4: Enable auto refresh in the report settings and set the refresh interval to 15 minutes.
column5: Create a Cloud Scheduler job to periodically reload the Looker Studio dashboard using the Looker Studio API.
column6: Configure a Pub/Sub trigger in BigQuery to push new findings data directly to Looker Studio in real-time.
column8: Looker Studio provides an auto refresh feature that periodically attempts to reload the data in a report. When enabled, you can configure the refresh interval, with options including 15 minutes. While the report is open, Looker Studio will automatically check for fresh data according to this interval. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/looker-studio/docs/manage-auto-refresh-for-a-report

column2: You are building an automated incident response workflow that sends Slack notifications when Security Command Center detects high-severity findings. You have configured a Pub/Sub topic and created a NotificationConfig in SCC. However, you notice that the Cloud Function is being triggered for all finding severities, not just high severity. What should you do to resolve this issue?
column3: Update the NotificationConfig filter to include severity = 'HIGH' AND state = 'ACTIVE' in the streaming_config.
column4: Create a separate Pub/Sub subscription with a message filter for high-severity findings.
column5: Modify the Cloud Function code to check the severity field in the Pub/Sub message payload and ignore non-high severity findings.
column6: Configure an IAM policy on the Pub/Sub topic to allow only high-severity findings to be published.
column8: The NotificationConfig includes a filter field that limits notifications to specific finding attributes. By adding severity = 'HIGH' AND state = 'ACTIVE' to the streaming_config filter, only high-severity active findings will be published to the Pub/Sub topic. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-api-manage-notifications

column2: Your organization wants to implement a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy that detects when the ratio of HTTP 5xx errors to total requests exceeds 5% for your security-critical API endpoints. You need to use a query-based approach that supports complex metric calculations. Which query language should you use to create this alerting policy?
column3: Use MQL to create an alerting policy that uses outer_join and ratio operations to calculate the error percentage.
column4: Create two separate metric-threshold alerting policies and use the Google Cloud console to combine them into a single ratio condition.
column5: Use PromQL to create a PromQL-based alerting policy that calculates the error ratio using rate functions and comparison operators.
column6: Configure a SQL-based alerting policy in Log Analytics that calculates the ratio using SQL aggregation functions on HTTP response logs.
column8: PromQL is the recommended query language for Cloud Monitoring and supports complex conditions including ratios, dynamic thresholds, and metric combinations. PromQL-based alerting policies can calculate ratios using functions like rate() and division operators, making it ideal for error rate calculations. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/promql/promql-in-alerting

column2: You are configuring Security Command Center to detect when cloud resources are accessed from IP addresses associated with known threat actors. Event Threat Detection uses Google's internal threat intelligence for IOC matching. However, your organization also subscribes to an external threat intelligence feed with additional malicious IP indicators. You need to incorporate these external IOCs into your detection strategy. What should you do?
column3: Enable Security Health Analytics to scan resource configurations against your external IOC list for potential compromise indicators.
column4: Upload your external threat intelligence feed directly to the SCC API and configure automatic IOC matching against all ingested logs.
column5: Create Event Threat Detection custom modules using the Configurable Bad IP template and populate them with IP addresses from your external threat intelligence feed.
column6: Configure continuous export of SCC findings to Google SecOps and use Applied Threat Intelligence to correlate with your external feed.
column8: Event Threat Detection custom modules allow you to extend detection capabilities with your own IOC data. The Configurable Bad IP module type lets you specify custom IP addresses that should trigger findings when observed in VPC Flow Logs, enabling integration of external threat intelligence with SCC's native detection. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: You are configuring a BigQuery-based threat detection solution. Your organization routes VPC Flow Logs and Cloud Audit Logs to BigQuery using log sinks. You have a threat intelligence table containing IOCs that is updated daily. You need to design a query solution that correlates logs from the past 24 hours with IOCs while minimizing query costs at scale. What should you do?
column3: Store logs in Cloud Storage using a log sink, then create BigQuery external tables with Hive partitioning for IOC matching queries.
column4: Configure the log sink to use date-sharded tables and query all tables using wildcard table functions with IOC JOINs.
column5: Create clustered tables by IP address fields and use BigQuery materialized views to pre-compute IOC matches daily.
column6: Use time-unit column partitioned tables for logs with daily granularity and require partition filters in queries that JOIN against the IOC table.
column8: Time-unit column partitioning enables BigQuery to prune partitions when queries filter on the partitioning column. Requiring partition filters ensures queries only scan relevant date partitions, significantly reducing query costs when JOINing with IOC data. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/partitioned-tables

column2: You are investigating a high-severity Container Threat Detection finding that shows 'Execution: Container Escape' in Security Command Center. The finding indicates that a known suspicious tool binary for container escape activities was executed in your GKE cluster. You need to gather additional context for your investigation. Which JSON field in the finding should you examine to identify the specific GKE node where the compromised Pod executed?
column3: resource.project_display_name
column4: VM_Instance_Name
column5: Pod_Namespace
column6: Container_Image_Uri
column8: The VM_Instance_Name field in the Container Threat Detection finding JSON contains the name of the GKE node where the Pod executed. This information is critical for understanding the scope of the potential compromise and identifying which node may require further investigation or remediation.
